title: 802.1X Port Authentication: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Plug in a cable, and you're on the network. Unless the door checks your I D first. That's eight oh two dot one X.

lines.t: Unless the door checks your ID

scenes.heading: The hotel key card system
scenes.narration: A guest, called the supplicant, arrives with their I D. The lift, which is the authenticator, won't move until they've been checked. It passes the I D along to the front desk, the authentication server, which is a RADIUS server. The front desk checks the booking records, and says yes or no. The lift just follows the answer. The lift never makes the decision itself.

scenes.heading: The sequence
scenes.narration: It runs in four steps. The device connects. The switch asks who it is, using E A P O L. The switch relays the answer to the server. The server says accept or reject, and the port opens or stays shut.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. The switch doesn't decide, the server does. E A P O L only runs between the device and the switch, and R A D I U S carries it onward. And eight oh two dot one X authenticates the supplicant on the device, which can still stand for a user.

items.wrong: EAPOL goes all the way to the server
items.right: Only to the switch; RADIUS carries it on
The supplicant can prove a user's identity

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Three roles: supplicant, authenticator and server. The port stays blocked until the server says yes. E A P O L is on the cable, and R A D I U S is behind the switch. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva 802.1X lab.

points.t: Port blocked until the server accepts
EAPOL on the wire, RADIUS behind the switch
